newsitem.title: GERMANY: French budget pact doubts raise fears in Germany.
newsitem.headline: French budget pact doubts raise fears in Germany.

text.p: Germany's worst fears about the Socialist victory in French elections appeared to materialise on Tuesday after Paris wasted no time in attacking a budget pact meant to ensure a stable European currency.
The so-called "stability pact", brainchild of German Finance Minister Theo Waigel, sets down tough budget goals and fines for nations living beyond their means after the euro is launched in 1999.

Francois Hollande, spokesman for France's Socialist party, told Reuters Financial Television late Monday night that the French government wanted to renegotiate the pact to among other things ensure it "does not signify new austerity in France."
Talk of fiddling with an agreement seen as key to ensuring a stable euro is the last thing that Bonn and the Bundesbank want to hear.
"Germany can't afford an abolition of the stability pact, not even small concessions," said Juergen Pfister, senior economist at Commerzbank.
Economists said the Bonn government, which has seen its EMU stability credentials come under attack of late, can ill afford even the appearance of substantive changes to the stability pact.

Broad outlines of the deal, agreed by European heads of state last year in Dublin, have been watered down from what Germany originally sought, they said, leaving little room for the pact to be further weakened.
"The stability pact as it stands now has plenty of loopholes," said Timo Klein, economist at MMS Internatinal in Frankfurt.
Waigel, facing calls for his resignation because of perceived weakness on EMU, cannot afford to make concessions that might lead to a softer euro.
France still has time to challenge the deal in Amsterdam on June 16 and 17 when the stability pact must be ratified by European heads of state.
But some analysts wondered how committed Paris was to rewriting the stability pact.
The socialists made creating jobs a top campaign issue and may now feel compelled to verbally attack the stability pact without really planning an all-out assult.
"This was a topic in the campaign and that is why the socialists are bringing it up now," said Holger Schmieding, economist at Merrill Lynch. "Germany is not going to back down through."
A spokesman at the Finance Ministry declined to comment on Hollande's remarks.
Economists said tough talk on the stability pact is symptomatic of larger problems between Bonn and Paris.

The socialists have spoken openly of allowing a wider membership in the first stage of EMU than Bonn is thought to favour and the creation of a political counterweight that could check the independence of the European central bank.
"There are clear areas of friction between Bonn and Paris now," Klein said. "There is a potential for conflict."
